h1: Paid brewery tours as a revenue line for a small brewery
title: Paid Brewery Tours as a Revenue Line | Craft Beer School
desc: How a small brewery can run paid tours: format, pricing sums, safety, licence questions and the staffing that stops tours from disrupting brew days.
teaser: A tour sells the one thing a can cannot: seeing where the beer comes from. Done badly, it also costs a brewer half a day.
standfirst: Guests will pay to walk through a brewery if the visit is well run. The money is real but modest. The risks sit on the brewhouse floor. Here is how to price a tour and keep it out of the brewer's way.
sections: What a paid tour actually sells

People do not pay to look at steel tanks. They pay for a story, a guide who knows the process and a taste of beer at the end. A good tour takes a guest from malt to glass in about 45 to 60 minutes, with something to smell or touch at each stop: a handful of crushed malt, a few hop pellets rubbed in the palm, a sample from the fermenter where your rules allow.

For a small brewery this is also marketing. Guests who stand next to the fermenters tend to become regulars and talk about the visit. The tour sits well beside brewing classes as a taproom revenue line, which sells the same curiosity at a higher price.

A simple running order works well: milling and malt, the mash and boil, fermentation, packaging, then the tasting. Keep each stop to about five minutes and let guests ask questions at the end of each, not all at the finish. Bring a printed card with the beer names and styles so guests can take something home.

Tasting on the premises depends on your licence. In India alcohol is a state subject, so what you may pour, in what quantity, at what hours and to whom differs between states and changes through notifications. A brewpub licence may allow service on site. A production-only licence may not. Ask a licensing consultant before you advertise a tour with tastings.

Never serve anyone under the legal drinking age. Many breweries run tours with a non-alcoholic option, which also suits guests who do not drink and groups with drivers.

Start with the cost of the hour, not with what other breweries charge. Here is an illustration with round, made up figures. A tour for 10 guests at ₹600 each earns ₹6,000. Take off the guide's time, the beer served (say ₹150 a head at your own cost) and cleaning afterwards. If those come to ₹3,000, the tour leaves ₹3,000. Eight such tours a month add up to ₹24,000 of contribution.

That is useful, not life changing. It becomes worthwhile when guests also buy food, beer to take away or merchandise on the same visit. Track spend per head, not only ticket sales.

Test your own prices with a few small groups and adjust. Fixed group sizes and advance booking make the sums much easier.

A brewery is a working site with hot surfaces, wet floors, steam, moving machinery and pressurised vessels. Guests are not trained for any of it. Set a fixed route with clear marked lines. Close off areas that cannot be made safe. Keep guests out of the cellar and the chemical store. Provide closed-toe shoes and tell people before they arrive.

Carbon dioxide collects at low levels in closed rooms, so keep tours out of fermentation cellars without good ventilation and an alarm. Our guide on a preventive maintenance plan for a brewery is relevant, because a tour makes worn hoses and loose guards visible to the public.

The worst tours happen when the brewer is mid-mash and a group walks in. Brew days need focus. A brewer talking to guests during a transfer is a recipe for a spill. Fix tour slots on the days and hours the brewhouse is quiet. Saturday afternoon often works for a pub because brewing is done in the morning or earlier in the week.

Decide who leads. A trained front-of-house guide can handle most visits. The brewer joins for questions at a set point. See brewery staffing for how small teams divide this kind of work.

Ask your insurance broker whether your policy covers visitors on the production floor. Do not assume it does. Ask too about group bookings by companies and about waiver forms. A simple written briefing at the start of the tour, with a signature, also records that guests were told the rules. This is not legal advice. Check with a broker or lawyer.

A paid tour works best as a small, steady stream tied to a bar or shop that can capture the visitor's spending afterwards. A brewery with no on-site sales needs a different plan. Brewery Business Management covers revenue lines like this one, with the costing needed to decide which ones deserve staff time.
faqs: Do I need a special licence to run brewery tours?
Tours with tastings depend on your state licence conditions. A consultant can tell you whether your licence allows on-site service and what limits apply.
How long should a brewery tour last?
Forty-five to sixty minutes is common. Longer tours need seating and a break.
Is it safe to bring the public into a brewhouse?
Yes, with a fixed route, supervision, closed-toe shoes and no access to cellars or chemical stores. CO2 and hot or wet floors are the main risks.
How should I price a brewery tour?
Work from your own costs: the guide's time, the beer served and cleaning. Then test the price on small groups.
